name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_STATEMENT_BASED_4_Q01 - Toxicity and excretion patterns of nitrogenous wastes

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements (I-IV) regarding excretory products and their elimination:

Statement I: Ammonia is the most toxic nitrogenous waste and requires a large amount of water for its elimination.

Statement II: Uric acid is the least toxic nitrogenous waste and can be removed with a minimum loss of water.

Statement III: Bony fishes excrete nitrogenous wastes as insoluble uric acid pellets through antennal glands.

Statement IV: Mammals, terrestrial amphibians, and marine fishes excrete uric acid and are called uricotelic animals.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Ammonia Toxicity and Hydration Demand
Ammonia is the most toxic common nitrogenous waste and is highly soluble in water, necessitating large volumes of fluid for diffusion across body or gill surfaces.

Step 2: Evaluation of Uric Acid Toxicity and Conservation Role
Uric acid possesses the lowest toxicity among common nitrogenous wastes and is virtually insoluble, allowing uricotelic animals to void it as a semi-solid paste or pellet to conserve water.

Step 3: Evaluation of Nitrogenous Waste and Organ in Bony Fishes
Bony fishes are ammonotelic and excrete ammonia as ammonium ions across gill surfaces; they do not excrete uric acid pellets, and antennal glands are found in crustaceans (such as prawns), not bony fishes.

Step 4: Evaluation of Mammalian and Amphibian Excretion Modes
Mammals, terrestrial amphibians, and marine fishes primarily excrete urea and are classified as ureotelic animals, not uricotelic.

Final Conceptual Answer: The propositions stating that ammonia is the most toxic waste requiring large water volumes and that uric acid is the least toxic waste requiring minimal water are biologically correct, whereas bony fishes excrete ammonia across gills and mammals are ureotelic.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_STATEMENT_BASED_4_Q02 - Morphometry and gross internal anatomy of kidney

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements (I-IV) regarding excretory products and their elimination:

Statement I: The human kidneys are bean-shaped structures situated along the anterior ventral wall between the cervical vertebrae and sacrum.

Statement II: Each kidney of an adult human measures 10-12 cm in length, 5-7 cm in width, and 2-3 cm in thickness.

Statement III: The average weight of an adult human kidney ranges between 120 and 170 grams.

Statement IV: The renal cortex extends in between the medullary pyramids as renal columns called Columns of Bertini.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Kidney Anatomical Location
Human kidneys lie retroperitoneally close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity between the last thoracic (T12) and third lumbar (L3) vertebrae, not along the anterior ventral wall or in cervical/sacral regions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Kidney Metric Dimensions
An adult human kidney measures 10 to 12 cm in length, 5 to 7 cm in width, and 2 to 3 cm in thickness.

Step 3: Evaluation of Kidney Gravimetric Range
The average mass of an adult human kidney is 120 to 170 grams.

Step 4: Evaluation of Renal Columns of Bertini
The cortex projects inward between adjacent conical medullary pyramids, forming the renal columns known as Columns of Bertini.

Final Conceptual Answer: The propositions detailing kidney dimensions (10-12 cm length), average weight (120-170 g), and Columns of Bertini are biologically correct, whereas kidneys lie retroperitoneally along the dorsal body wall between T12 and L3.

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements (I-IV) regarding excretory products and their elimination:

Statement I: Blood from the glomerulus is carried away by an efferent arteriole.

Statement II: Glomerulus along with Bowman's capsule is called the Malpighian body or renal corpuscle.

Statement III: Cortical nephrons possess very long loops of Henle dipping deeply into the inner medulla with prominent vasa recta.

Statement IV: The collecting ducts converge and open into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids in the calyces.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Glomerular Outflow Vasculature
The glomerular capillary tuft is drained by an efferent arteriole, which subsequently branches into peritubular capillaries and vasa recta.

Step 2: Evaluation of Malpighian Corpuscle Components
The double-walled Bowman's capsule and enclosed glomerulus together constitute the renal corpuscle (Malpighian body).

Step 3: Evaluation of Cortical Nephron Features
In cortical nephrons, the loop of Henle is short and extends only minimally into the medulla, with vasa recta being absent or highly reduced; long loops dipping deep into the medulla with prominent vasa recta characterize juxtamedullary nephrons.

Step 4: Evaluation of Collecting Duct Convergence
Distal convoluted tubules drain into collecting ducts, which pass through the medullary pyramids and converge to empty into the calyces of the renal pelvis.

Final Conceptual Answer: The propositions identifying the efferent arteriole, Malpighian corpuscle components, and collecting duct convergence into the renal pelvis are correct, whereas cortical nephrons have short loops of Henle with reduced vasa recta.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_STATEMENT_BASED_4_Q04 - Ultrafiltration dynamics and filtration membrane layers

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements (I-IV) regarding excretory products and their elimination:

Statement I: Glomerular filtration is carried out by the glomerulus using the glomerular capillary blood pressure.

Statement II: On an average, 1100-1200 mL of blood is filtered by the human kidneys per minute.

Statement III: The glomerular capillary blood pressure causes filtration of blood through three distinct layers forming the filtration membrane.

Statement IV: The epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule called podocytes leave minute spaces called filtration slits or slit pores.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Driving Pressure for Ultrafiltration
Hydrostatic blood pressure within the glomerular capillaries provides the driving force that forces fluid across the filtration barrier into Bowman's capsule.

Step 2: Evaluation of Renal Blood Perfusion Rate
The kidneys filter approximately 1100 to 1200 mL of blood per minute, representing about one-fifth of ventricular cardiac output.

Step 3: Evaluation of Filtration Membrane Architecture
The filtration membrane consists of three structural layers: fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium, basement membrane, and visceral epithelium of Bowman's capsule.

Step 4: Evaluation of Podocyte Slit Pores
Podocytes wrap around glomerular capillaries with interdigitating foot processes, leaving tiny gaps designated as filtration slits or slit pores.

Final Conceptual Answer: All four propositions regarding glomerular capillary pressure, renal perfusion volume (1100-1200 mL/min), three-layered filtration barrier, and podocyte slit pores are biologically correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_STATEMENT_BASED_4_Q05 - Tubular reabsorption and active transport mechanisms

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements (I-IV) regarding excretory products and their elimination:

Statement I: Nearly 99 per cent of the glomerular filtrate formed daily is reabsorbed by the renal tubules.

Statement II: Substances like glucose, amino acids, and Na+ in the filtrate are reabsorbed actively.

Statement III: Nitrogenous wastes like urea are reabsorbed by active transport against steep concentration gradients.

Statement IV: Tubular secretion of hydrogen and potassium ions drives systemic blood into severe acidosis.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Total Tubular Reabsorption Fraction
Of the 180 litres of ultrafiltrate formed each day, approximately 178.5 litres (nearly 99%) is reabsorbed along the nephron, producing about 1.5 litres of urine.

Step 2: Evaluation of Active Reabsorption of Nutrients and Sodium
Essential organic metabolites (glucose, amino acids) and major sodium ions are transported back into peritubular blood via active transport mechanisms.

Step 3: Evaluation of Nitrogenous Waste Transport Mechanism
Nitrogenous wastes such as urea are reabsorbed passively down concentration gradients, not actively.

Step 4: Evaluation of Tubular Secretion Physiological Role
Selective secretion of H⁺, K⁺, and ammonia into the tubular lumen maintains blood pH and electrolyte homeostasis; it prevents acidosis rather than causing severe acidosis.

Final Conceptual Answer: The propositions stating that nearly 99% of filtrate is reabsorbed and that glucose, amino acids, and sodium are reabsorbed actively are correct, whereas nitrogenous wastes diffuse passively and tubular secretion maintains physiological pH balance.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_STATEMENT_BASED_4_Q06 - Differential permeability and counter current multiplier

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements (I-IV) regarding excretory products and their elimination:

Statement I: The descending limb of Henle's loop is completely impermeable to water and actively extrudes sodium chloride.

Statement II: The ascending limb of Henle's loop is impermeable to water but allows transport of electrolytes actively or passively.

Statement III: The proximity and counter current flow in Henle's loop and vasa recta maintain an increasing medullary osmolarity from 300 to 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹.

Statement IV: The medullary hyperosmolar gradient is mainly caused and maintained by NaCl and urea.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Descending Limb Transport Properties
The descending limb of Henle's loop is freely permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, losing water osmotically to concentrate the filtrate; it does not actively extrude NaCl.

Step 2: Evaluation of Ascending Limb Transport Properties
The ascending limb is impermeable to water, allowing electrolytes (NaCl) to exit passively in the thin segment and actively in the thick segment, diluting the luminal fluid.

Step 3: Evaluation of Medullary Osmolar Gradient Range
The counter current multiplier arrangement elevates interstitial osmolarity from 300 mOsmol L⁻¹ in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹ in the inner medulla.

Step 4: Evaluation of Primary Solutes Generating Hypertonicity
Accumulation of sodium chloride transported by the ascending limb and urea recycled from the collecting duct generates the medullary concentration gradient.

Final Conceptual Answer: The propositions regarding water impermeability of the ascending limb, medullary osmolarity rising from 300 to 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹, and NaCl and urea causing the gradient are correct, whereas the descending limb is permeable to water and impermeable to electrolytes.

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements (I-IV) regarding excretory products and their elimination:

Statement I: A fall in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure, or GFR activates juxtaglomerular cells to release renin.

Statement II: Renin converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I and further to angiotensin II.

Statement III: Angiotensin II acts as a powerful vasodilator that lowers systemic blood pressure and reduces GFR.

Statement IV: Aldosterone causes reabsorption of Na+ and water from the distal parts of the tubule, elevating blood pressure and GFR.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Renin Release Stimulus
Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells in the afferent arteriole respond to decreased perfusion pressure or reduced GFR by secreting renin into the bloodstream.

Step 2: Evaluation of Angiotensin Conversion Cascade
Renin enzymatically cleaves circulating angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, which is converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme.

Step 3: Evaluation of Angiotensin II Vascular Actions
Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor that elevates arteriolar resistance and glomerular hydrostatic pressure, increasing GFR; it is not a vasodilator and does not lower blood pressure.

Step 4: Evaluation of Aldosterone Epithelial Actions
Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex, which acts on distal tubules to reabsorb sodium and water, raising blood volume, pressure, and GFR.

Final Conceptual Answer: The propositions detailing renin release by JG cells, the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin II, and aldosterone-mediated sodium and water reabsorption are correct, whereas angiotensin II acts as a vasoconstrictor that elevates blood pressure and GFR.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_STATEMENT_BASED_4_Q08 - Endocrine regulation by ADH and atrial natriuretic factor

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements (I-IV) regarding excretory products and their elimination:

Statement I: Excessive loss of fluid activates osmoreceptors, stimulating the release of ADH from the neurohypophysis.

Statement II: ADH facilitates water reabsorption from the latter parts of the tubule, thereby preventing diuresis.

Statement III: An increase in blood flow to the atria of the heart causes the release of Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF).

Statement IV: ANF causes vasodilation of blood vessels and thereby decreases blood pressure, acting as a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Hypothalamic Osmoreceptor Activation
Dehydration or hypovolemia stimulates hypothalamic osmoreceptors, triggering the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, or vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary.

Step 2: Evaluation of ADH Antidiuretic Mechanism
ADH increases water permeability in the late DCT and collecting duct, promoting water retention and preventing diuresis.

Step 3: Evaluation of ANF Secretory Trigger
Elevated atrial stretch resulting from increased venous return or high blood volume prompts cardiac atria to release Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF).

Step 4: Evaluation of ANF Hemodynamic Counter-Regulation
ANF relaxes vascular smooth muscle (vasodilation) and promotes urinary sodium loss, lowering blood pressure and serving as an antagonistic check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.

Final Conceptual Answer: All four propositions regarding ADH release upon fluid loss, ADH-mediated water retention, atrial ANF release, and ANF-induced vasodilation checking RAAS are biologically correct.
